evidence.text: The site analyzes the oracle form of 老 as a bent person with long hair and a staff (丨); in bronze forms the staff is written 匕, later also miswritten 止. It reports oracle-bone use as a place name in 合集22246, bronze uses for an elderly person, the adjective ‘old’, senior ministers, and ‘father’ written 老 for 考. It notes spring-and-autumn graphic variation and says one variant may have a phonetic role, but does not establish this as the graph’s original formation.
evidence.title: 漢語甲骨部件分析: 老

evidence.source: ShuoWen.org, 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The Eastern Han Shuowen account glosses 老 as 考, says a person aged seventy is called 老, and analyzes the form as 人、毛、匕, explaining white hair. Duan Yucai notes debate around 轉注 and quotes Dai Zhen’s account of 老 and 考 as mutually glossing words; Duan also argues the small-seal form may derive from 毛匕, with 人 not a separate element. This is a later lexicographic analysis, not direct confirmation of the oracle graph’s origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「老」

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The entry repeats the Shuowen explanation, provides modern Mandarin lǎo, and lists senses including old person, old in age, respectful address for elders or high-status people, respect elders, long-standing/old, retired, experienced, frequent/intensifying uses and prefix uses. Its quotations include Warring States texts such as Zhanguo Ce and Mencius, but the entry does not establish a full chronology for those semantic extensions.
evidence.title: A03251 老 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.text: Local row for 老 gives modern Mandarin lǎo, Middle Chinese lawX, Old Chinese *C.rˤuʔ, GSR 1055a, gloss ‘old’. This is local dataset evidence; the inspected web sources do not provide a click-through for this row.

evidence.text: Local row for 考 gives modern Mandarin kǎo, Middle Chinese khawX, Old Chinese *k-r̥ˤuʔ, GSR 1041d, gloss ‘old; deceased father’. In this system the initial and notation differ from 老 *C.rˤuʔ; the rows must not be silently merged. This supports a historical phonological comparison but does not by itself prove an etymological cognate relation.

evidence.text: The entry reports the earliest cited oracle usage as a place name (合集22246), so that instance does not itself attest the lexical sense ‘old’. Bronze inscriptions are cited for ‘elderly person’, ‘be old’, senior statesmen, and 老 used for 考 ‘father’. Warring States bamboo-text citations include ‘舜乃老’ (‘Shun then grew old’) and ‘老夫’, where ‘old’ need not be literal. These are the source’s reported examples; their original artifacts/text editions were not separately inspected here.

gaps: No glyph images were visually inspected. Paleographic descriptions are reported from CUHK's textual analysis.

The CUHK page’s earliest cited oracle instance uses 老 as a place name; the relation of that to the lexical ‘old’ sense is not established in the inspected evidence. No absolute dated artifact for that inscription was recovered.

The dossier calls the formation pictographic/ideographic and offers a modern cane mnemonic. CUHK supports a pictographic interpretation of the oracle form, while Shuowen gives a later component analysis; the precise sequence of graphic changes and any alleged corruption beyond the staff’s changing shape remains incompletely documented.

The semantic relation between ‘old’ and ‘father’ in the 老-for-考 bronze use is not established. The Shuowen reciprocal gloss and traditional 轉注 association are historical scholarly claims, not a demonstrated semantic chronology.

Potential 孝 comparison is not evidence of a phonetic component in 老. Baxter–Sagart values are preserved as that system’s own rows; current Unihan readings are metadata only, not evidence of an ancient sound relationship.
Official Unicode Unihan character pages could not be inspected despite real direct attempts, so click-through references are provided but their current page contents are unverified.
